clinicalPearls: Survival depends on early recognition, high-quality chest compressions, early defibrillation of shockable rhythms, and prompt treatment of reversible causes
Prioritise minimally interrupted, good-quality compressions of adequate depth and rate, allowing full chest recoil

Rapidly determine whether the rhythm is shockable (ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia) or non-shockable (asystole or pulseless electrical activity), as this directs the algorithm
Defibrillate shockable rhythms without delay and resume compressions immediately after each shock
Systematically seek and correct the reversible causes, remembered as the four Hs and four Ts
Effective teamwork, clear leadership, and minimising pauses around rhythm checks and shocks improve outcomes
After return of spontaneous circulation, focus on post-resuscitation care: oxygenation and ventilation targets, haemodynamic support, and identifying the underlying cause
In traumatic arrest, address the specific reversible causes such as hypovolaemia, tension pneumothorax, and tamponade rather than relying on standard medical algorithms alone
reference.pathophysiology: Cardiac arrest is the sudden cessation of effective cardiac output. Shockable rhythms arise from disorganised (ventricular fibrillation) or excessively rapid (pulseless ventricular tachycardia) electrical activity that prevents coordinated contraction, most often on a background of ischaemic heart disease. Non-shockable arrest reflects either absent electrical activity (asystole) or organised electrical activity without a pulse (pulseless electrical activity), commonly due to a profound reversible insult. Regardless of mechanism, cessation of circulation causes global ischaemia; the brain tolerates only minutes before injury begins, so restoration of perfusion by chest compressions and treatment of the cause is time-critical.
additionalDifferentials: Reversible causes: hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperkalaemia and metabolic disorders, hypothermia
Reversible causes: tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis (coronary or pulmonary)
Profound bradyarrhythmia or heart block preceding arrest
Traumatic cardiac arrest with mechanism-specific causes
additionalInvestigations: Continuous rhythm analysis and cardiac monitoring throughout resuscitation
Point-of-care blood gas, potassium, and glucose to identify reversible metabolic causes
Bedside ultrasound to assess for tamponade, hypovolaemia, and cardiac activity during rhythm checks
Waveform capnography to confirm airway placement and gauge resuscitation quality and return of circulation
Post-arrest 12-lead ECG and coronary assessment when a cardiac cause is suspected
redFlags: A shockable rhythm requiring immediate defibrillation, where every minute of delay reduces survival
Failure to identify and treat a reversible cause (the four Hs and four Ts)
Prolonged interruptions in chest compressions degrading perfusion
Tension pneumothorax, tamponade, or major haemorrhage as an immediately treatable cause in traumatic arrest
Post-resuscitation hypoxia, hypotension, or hyperthermia worsening neurological outcome
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the initial rhythm, the promptness of high-quality resuscitation and defibrillation, and whether a reversible cause is corrected. Witnessed shockable arrests with early bystander CPR and defibrillation have the best prognosis, whereas unwitnessed asystolic arrest and prolonged downtime carry poor survival and higher risk of neurological injury.
pitfalls: Interrupting chest compressions excessively for rhythm checks, intubation, or vascular access
Delaying defibrillation of a shockable rhythm
Focusing on drugs and airway while neglecting the search for reversible causes
Applying standard medical algorithms to traumatic arrest without treating haemorrhage, tension pneumothorax, and tamponade
Neglecting structured post-resuscitation care after return of spontaneous circulation
management: High-quality, minimally interrupted chest compressions of adequate depth and rate with full chest recoil
Early defibrillation of shockable rhythms (ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia) with immediate resumption of compressions after each shock
Adrenaline for all arrests, with amiodarone or lidocaine for refractory shockable rhythms
Systematic identification and correction of the reversible causes, the four Hs and four Ts
Airway management with waveform capnography to confirm placement and gauge resuscitation quality and return of circulation
Post-resuscitation care with targeted temperature management, coronary assessment and organ support once circulation returns
Clear team leadership minimising pauses around rhythm checks and shocks, with structured escalation and prognostication
